stories.headline: AFL overreactions: The Swans spent all of their emotional tickets in their stirring qualifying final
stories.summary: The Swans shocked the footy world when they smashed the Brisbane Lions in their qualifying final, but have they spent all their emotional tickets after a challenging month? It's time to react to the week's big talking point.
stories.body:
There are plenty of talking points after the AFL's semifinal weekend, with one of the biggest being whether the Swans can back up after such a breathtaking performance against Brisbane in their qualifying final.

Let's get to this week's overreactions column, where we judge the biggest takeaways as legitimate or irrational.

The Swans spent all of their emotional tickets in their stirring qualifying final win
Almost nobody gave Sydney a chance of knocking off back-to-back reigning premier Brisbane in their qualifying final at the SCG. The club was reeling in the aftermath of one of its biggest scandals in history, having dumped five players for their involvement in the Pullman Hotel saga, and appeared a prime candidate to depart finals in straight sets.

And yet for two-and-a-half hours they embarrassed the Lions, booting 21 goals to win by 53 points in one of the most unexpected, electric performances in recent finals history. Now a preliminary final date with minor premier Fremantle at the SCG awaits. Win that and it will be a sixth Grand Final appearance in 16 years and a third in the last five years.

Verdict: Overreaction

The question on everyone's mind ahead of Friday night's clash against the Dockers is whether the Swans spent too much emotional energy in that stirring win over Brisbane. It truly was a backs-against-the-wall type performance, the kind of unexpected victory that can lift an entire football club, and its fanbase, out of its mire.

Of course, I'm speculating and this is only a hunch, but I think they can keep the momentum rolling. Call me crazy, but I'd be far more concerned if Sydney had to back up the following week. Instead, the Swans players have been able to put their feet up for two weeks, gently float back down to earth after what was such an incredible high, and then switch their focus to their preliminary final task at hand.

Adelaide just showed us how an emotion-sapping win can come back to bite you the following week. The Crows held off the Bulldogs at home in a cutthroat elimination final last week, a game that reportedly saved Matthew Nicks' future and was a farewell to Taylor Walker's Adelaide Oval career, only to be thrashed seven days later by the Lions. Of course, the Lions are a competition benchmark, but the Crows' first five minutes looked like a team 'out of tickets'.

You also have to love how so many Swans either found form or carried on their purple patches against Brisbane last time out. Logan McDonald played the game of his life, kicking a career-high six goals. Charlie Curnow and Tom Papley were both electric with five goals apiece. And Errol Gulden might be the most in-form man in the competition.

With all due respect to the Dockers, beating Fremantle at the SCG isn't a more difficult task than beating Brisbane at the SCG.

-- Jake Michaels

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey draft picks: Grab these defenseman before their breakout year
stories.summary: Everyone's looking for a breakout season before it happens. Here are the defensemen with the right opportunities.
stories.body:
Darren Raddysh is the exception, not the rule. He's not what we are looking for. A 30-year-old defender launching from 1.32 fantasy points per game to 2.29 fantasy points per game happens about as often as a leap year. What we are after is what happens more often. We are leaning into the "usual."

As in, usually "a defenseman has played X number of games and are usually X years old when they start to contribute to fantasy hockey."

Here's the quick line to what I'm defining as "usual."

The median fantasy points per game (FPPG) across the 1,020 individual top-60 defense seasons since 2009-10 is 1.89, so that's the bar we set for a breakout.

Using all game logs since the 2009-10 season, there are 162 defenders that have made more than one appearance among the top 60 for fantasy scoring. This purposefully excludes any one-time flukes.

Of those 162 defenders, 98 made their debut in 2009-10 or later, meaning we have complete game logs for their entire career.

Of those 98 defenders, 73 eventually held a rolling 41-game FPPG average above 1.89 for at least 41 consecutive games -- a half-season at that pace at minimum, and often longer.

The average age those 73 blue-liners had reached when that breakout run began was 24 years, 248 days (with the majority doing it between 22 years, 330 days and 26 years, 266 days).

The average experience those 73 D had when that run began was 254 games played (with the majority doing it between 157 and 379).

So Raddysh is unusual.

He didn't make the list of 73 because he hasn't had multiple top-60 fantasy seasons. He will after this season, but that's not the point. The point is that only a half a dozen D-men since the 2009-10 season have burst onto the scene when they are as old as Raddysh. By the numbers, we want to look for younger players when hoping for a breakout.

What's interesting though is when you consider the other half of the formula: Experience.

Raddysh has a career 249 games played, which is only five games shy of the "usual" breakout experience for the 73 defenders that made the breakout list. Age is important, but it clearly isn't the only factor. Raddysh didn't make his debut until he was 25 and didn't play his first full season until he was 27.

So we flip Raddysh's profile around. Instead of a player who arrived late and spiked out of nowhere, we're hunting the defenders sitting right in that pocket. Young enough that the breakout is probably still ahead of them, experienced enough that they're due. And to keep this list actually useful, I've thrown out anyone who's already posted a top-60 fantasy season on the blue line. We're not looking for guys who've done it before; we're looking for the ones who haven't done it yet.

More: Sign up for free | Rankings | Projections | League types

The breakouts

Philip Broberg, D, St. Louis Blues (25.2 years old, 1.14 FPPG in 230 games played): Broberg is already a heavy-minutes, underlying-metrics darling and the only thing capping his fantasy value is a power play he's never truly run. With Justin Faulk now in Detroit, that quarterback job is finally open. Win it over Logan Mailloux and the 50-point breakout arrives; lose it and he's a multi-category floor play.

Jamie Drysdale, D, Philadelphia Flyers (24.4 years old, 1.23 FPPG in 295 games played): Drysdale took a step last season (32 points), got a new four-year deal for it, and opens 2026-27 quarterbacking Philadelphia's top power play. The 50-point ceiling is live if he seizes true top-pairing minutes. The recurring "if" is health, which has interrupted every prior run at a breakout.

Owen Power, D, Buffalo Sabres (23.8 years old, 1.39 FPPG in 323 games played): The former No. 1 pick has the pedigree and the minutes but keeps refusing to shoot, as he managed zero power-play points last season despite getting 75 minutes there. Power has shown he can play defense, the key will be him deciding to chip in on offense once in a while, too.

Luke Hughes, D, New Jersey Devils (23.0 years old, 1.39 FPPG in 223 games played): Even splitting the top power play with Dougie Hamilton, Hughes ranked 14th among qualified defensemen (minimum 1:15 per game) in power-play points per 60 last season -- elite rate production that just needs more time to become raw totals. Hamilton keeps it a committee, but the per-minute scoring says Hughes doesn't need the whole job to pay off.

Pavel Mintyukov, D, Anaheim Ducks (22.8 years old, 1.33 FPPG in 204 games played): Anaheim bet five years and $36 million on Mintyukov's upside, and a rising even-strength role should push him past 20 minutes a night with triple-digit blocks and shots. The catch is the power play. Jackson LaCombe owns the top unit, so unless Mintyukov pries it loose, his point ceiling stays capped and he's more floor than fireworks.

J.J. Moser, D, Tampa Bay Lightning (26.2 years old, 1.34 FPPG in 338 games played): Fittingly, Moser spent last season paired with the very same Darren Raddysh from our intro, the two forming one of the NHL's stingiest shutdown duos. He'll get to run it back this year as the shutdown side of the top pairing with either Victor Hedman or John Carlson. The question now is whether he can layer the shot-blocking and hits from his Coyotes days back onto the big minutes and points he's found in Tampa.

ESPN Fantasy Hockey is the fun, free way to get inside the game. Draft your players, set your lineups and earn points when the pros do. Sign up today!

Already broken out

These defenders already cracked the top 60 in a season, so they're not breakouts in the strict sense, but they sit right in the same age-and-experience wheelhouse as the names above. Several are still going under-appreciated on draft day relative to what they already produce. Consider them the safer, proven cousins of the bets we just made.

Bowen Byram, D, Chicago Blackhawks (25.2 years old, 1.46 FPPG in 331 games played): Byram's move to Chicago gives him a real shot at the offensive keys he could never fully hold in Buffalo or Colorado. Just know he'll have to hold off the young Blackhawks blue line for the power-play reps. The counting stats are proven, but the top-unit role isn't handed to him.

Mattias Samuelsson, D, Buffalo Sabres (26.5 years old, 2.01 FPPG in 292 games played): Ignore the shiny plus-41 that inflated last year's rate, it won't repeat, and it's an increasingly rare fantasy category anyway. The reason to roster Samuelsson is the floor beneath it, as he led the Sabres in blocked shots and ranked among their top hitters. This is the kind of every-night volume that quietly wins the peripheral categories a lot of managers punt.

Brandt Clarke, D, Los Angeles Kings (23.6 years old, 2.02 FPPG in 188 games played): Clarke is the youngest name here and the most complete offensive package. The 23-year-old is a legitimate power-play performer already producing at a top-tier rate, and now stepping fully out of Drew Doughty's shadow to run the Kings' back end as his own.

Simon Edvinsson, D, Detroit Red Wings (23.6 years old, 1.77 FPPG in 177 games played): Two of the 60 most physical seasons any defenseman 23-or-younger has posted since 2009-10 belong to Edvinsson, and he's played only two full ones, with his workload still climbing. He pairs with Moritz Seider, a star in his own right who tops that very list, giving Detroit a young shutdown tandem that already floods the hits-and-blocks columns; the points will follow as the minutes do.

Braden Schneider, D, New York Rangers (24.9 years old, 1.42 FPPG in 372 games played): Schneider turns up on that same list as Edvinsson -- one of the most physical young-defenseman seasons since 2009-10 -- which is the whole case for him: hits, blocks, and a quietly growing point total that add up to more than the zero fantasy buzz he gets behind the Rangers' bigger names. He won't win you a category, but he's the steady multi-cat piece that outproduces his draft slot.

stories.headline: Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

The drivers will be racing around a circuit that has been purpose-built for the occasion.

- What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records

She's an active runner and does boxing with a focus on general fitness content as well.

The Instagram account is full of content following the next generation of go-karts.

Based in America, he's a car photographer and has over one million followers on Instagram.

He's an actor, writer and digital content creator from Hong Kong.

Mike Dokas

His TikTok channel mainly focuses on football and Formula 1 content. He has over 350,000 followers on the platform.

AustrianKiwi (Jonathan Balchin) - Comedian

He makes funny and relatable videos around daily life in Austria.

He's from New Zealand but lives in Australia and has over one million followers on Instagram. His videos are based on comedy including filming behind the scenes on the Avengers and references to Toy Story.

He's a digital content creator, streamer from Brazil and blew up through viral reaction videos. He has nearly 12 million followers on Instagram.

From China, his content online features lots of cars and car culture.

Enis Kirazoğlu - Content Creator

TheGrefg - Streamer and Content Creator

He's one of Spain's biggest gaming creators and is particularly known for Fortnite with 12.29 million followers on Twitch and 19.9 million followers on YouTube. In 2021, more than 2.4 million people tuned in to the reveal of his Fortnite skin, which set a Guinness World Record for concurrent viewers on an individual Twitch stream at the time.

Caedrel (Marc Lamont) - Streamer

In 2024, he founded esports organisation Los Ratones and has become one of the biggest personalities in the LoL community.

TheDonato (Donato José Muñoz Calabres) - Streamer and Content Creator

TheDonato is a Venezuelan Red Bull partnered gaming creator who built a huge following through games including Garena Free Fire. He has more than 40 million subscribers on YouTube, with the creator himself crediting his switch to Free Fire as a major turning point in his career.

Helydia (Celia Tansel) - Streamer and Content Creator

Helydia is a French Valorant player and streamer who has built her community through competitive gaming content on Twitch and YouTube. She's also a Red Bull player and regularly takes part in Valorant showmatches and gaming events.

Diogo 'MoveMind' da Silva - Streamer and Content Creator

MoveMind is one of Portugal's best-known streamers and started broadcasting on Twitch as a hobby in 2017. He first broke through while commentating on matches involving professional Portuguese FIFA players and has since made the transition from reporting on esports and virtual FIFA matches to live sports broadcasting of real football games.

Jonathan Amaral - Professional Esports Player

Better known as Jonathan Gaming, Amaral is one of India's leading mobile esports players and is best known for competing in BGMI and PUBG Mobile. In 2026, he launched his own esports organisation, Team Apex Gaming.

RDJavi (Steven Javier Santos del Rosario) - Streamer

RDJavi is a Dominican streamer and gaming YouTuber known widely for his gaming content, particularly GTA V, GTA Roleplay, and automotive vlogs.

TechnoGamerz - Gaming Content Creator

Ujjwal Chaurasia, better known as Techno Gamerz, is one of India's biggest gaming creators and is particularly known for his GTA V content. In 2026, he became the first individual gaming creator in India and all of Asia to pass 50 million subscribers on YouTube.

Amar - Streamer and Entertainer

Amar Al-Naimi, better known as AmarCoDTV, is one of the leading figures in Germany's streaming scene, with content centred around gaming and entertainment. His background includes competitive Call of Duty, while Fortnite has also become a major part of his streaming career.

Nugato - Streamer

Ilija 'Nugato' Ravlić is a Croatian gamer and YouTuber who started creating content in 2013. He became particularly known for Minecraft videos and is now part of Red Bull's gaming roster.

iiTzTimmy (Timothy An) - Streamer

Timothy An, better known as iiTzTimmy, is an American streamer and professional Apex Legends competitor. He's known for marathon gaming challenges, including a Solo Bronze to Predator 34-hour stream that went viral where he went from Rookie to Predator in 126 games.

Qucee (Quentin Correia) - Streamer

Qucee is a Dutch YouTuber, rapper and streamer who is also part of the Supergaande collective. His content has included comedy, street interviews, freestyle rap and live-streaming.

Leticia Bufoni - Professional Skateboarder

Bufoni is a six-time X Games gold medallist, a former world No. 1 and 2015 SLS Super Crown Champion. She holds multiple Guinness World Records and represented Brazil at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. From go-karting in her youth she's since added motor racing to her résumé and competes in Porsche Cup Brazil, so she could be one to watch on the track.

Sarah Vignot Lezito - Stunt Rider

Sarah Vignot, known professionally as Sarah Lezito is a world-famous French motorcycle stunt rider who began practising her craft as a teenager. Her riding skills have also taken her to Hollywood, where she has performed motorcycle stunt work in major films as a movie stunt double.

Arda Saatçi - Ultra Athlete

Known as 'Cyborg', Saatçi is a German-Turkish extreme endurance athlete and Red Bull Athlete who specialises in extreme endurance challenges. He initially wanted to become a professional footballer, playing for Berliner AK U19 and SV Altlüdersdorf in his youth before injury led him towards endurance sport.

Lethal Shooter (Chris Matthews) - NBA Shooting Coach

Matthews is a former professional basketball player and Red Bull partner who is now one of the sport's most sought-after shooting coaches. Known as 'Lethal Shooter', he's worked with players from both the NBA and WNBA to improve their shooting.

Janja Garnbret - Professional Climber

Garnbret is widely regarded as one of the greatest competition climbers of all time. The Slovenian is a two-time Olympic champion, has won 10 world titles and over 50 World Cup gold medals. In 2026 she recorded her 50th World Cup victory.

Leo Neugebauer - Decathlon World Champion

Neugebauer is a German track and field athlete who won the decathlon world title for Germany in Tokyo in 2025 after previously taking silver at the Paris Olympics. He holds the German national records for both the outdoor decathlon (8,961 points) and the indoor heptathlon as well as taking the men's decathlon title at the Birmingham 2026 European Athletics Championships.

Molly Carlson - Professional Cliff Diver

Carlson is a Canadian high diver, Red Bull cliff diving athlete and a three-time World Championship silver medalist (2022, 2023, and 2024). She's also built a huge online community through her #BraveGang movement to encourage self-love, body positivity, and overcoming fears.

Matt Jones (Matthew Jones) - Red Bull MTB Athlete

Jones is a professional British mountain bike (MTB) freeride and slopestyle athlete. He broke onto the international scene in 2013 and has become known for pushing the limits of the sport with innovative tricks and riding projects.

Billy Bolt - Motorcycle Racer

Bolt should certainly be comfortable with speed as he's a world-renowned, six-time FIM SuperEnduro world champion. The British rider also won the inaugural FIM Hard Enduro World Championship in 2021.

Aidan Heslop - Cliff Diver

Heslop is a British-Welsh high diver who won the men's 27m world title in 2024 at the World Aquatics Championships in Doha. That same year, he was crowned Red Bull Cliff Diving World Series champion after winning four stops during the season.

Pol Tarrés - Enduro Rider

stories.headline: How Team USA rallied to beat France and win World Cup gold
stories.summary: France led by 14 points early, but the U.S. defense dominated and veterans stepped up to capture a fifth straight gold.
stories.body:
The U.S. women's basketball team has not lost a game in major international play since 2006 and has lost only one gold medal game (in 1983). Yet when the Americans faced a double-digit deficit in the first half of the FIBA Women's World Cup final Sunday, they couldn't just rely on history.

They had to get it done on court.

Team USA beat France 97-79 in Berlin to win its fifth consecutive World Cup title and 12th overall. Trailing 45-43 at halftime, the Americans took control in the third quarter, outscoring France 30-12. That dominance decided the game and the gold medal.

Coming in, France had been the more impressive team in the tournament, winning its five games by an average of 35.6 points with no margin closer than 22. Team USA, by contrast, beat Italy in group play by three points and Spain in the semifinals by 10. A strong start Sunday kept the momentum on France's side.

But then the U.S. defense took it up a notch in the second half, and the offense followed. The mojo changed entirely in the Americans' favor, with multiple players stepping forward.

Stars such as four-time WNBA MVP A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum were out due to injuries. That led to seven of the 12 U.S. players competing in their first major 5-on-5 international competition, including Rhyne Howard, Aliyah Boston, Caitlin Clark and Paige Bueckers, the past four WNBA Rookie of the Year award winners.

But the veterans supplemented all the "new," led by Jackie Young, Breanna Stewart, Chelsea Gray, Kahleah Copper and Napheesa Collier. Young, who had 18 points, six rebounds and five assists, was Sunday's player of the game. Stewart, who had 22 points, 10 rebounds and four assists, was MVP of the tournament.

Now the WNBA players from all the teams in this tournament head back to finish the regular season and get ready for the playoffs. But here's how Team USA stayed on top of the world and denied France its first World Cup gold.

How did Team USA go from trailing by 14 points to winning by 18?

Voepel: Defense. France was getting the shots it wanted and making them in the first half. That had been the case throughout this tournament, as the French offense had controlled all its previous games.

That changed in the second half, as the U.S. women relied on both their individual defensive strengths and their ability to switch without losing anything in their matchups. Everything the Americans did in the third quarter defensively was sharper, quicker and more focused. Not surprisingly, forcing France into missed shots and turnovers fueled the Americans' offense.

U.S. coach Kara Lawson is known as a defensive coach at Duke, and U.S. assistant Natalie Nakase guides the WNBA's top defensive team, the Golden State Valkyries. That expertise on the bench and the defensive strengths of the Americans' veterans turned around the game.

Stewart told TNT after the game that even when the Americans were down 14, they really weren't rattled. The fact that they cut the deficit to two by halftime -- a big steal by Angel Reese led to a 3-pointer by Clark before the buzzer -- gave the team a boost. And the Americans looked very confident starting the third quarter. Those 10 minutes made all the difference.

Philippou: Lawson said the second quarter might have been her favorite of the game. The U.S. women still trailed by two when the period ended, but the momentum had shifted in their favor -- especially after those plays from Reese and Clark -- and they had started to figure out some things. Once they got into the locker room, they could home in on how to fix the defensive lapses that plagued them early on.

At halftime, Stewart said, Lawson told the players that France might stay with them for three quarters, but by the time they got to the fourth, the United States was going to be able to bust things open. "Little do we know," Stewart said, "it came in the third quarter."

And before long, Team USA looked to have regained the psychological edge, getting whatever it wanted on both ends. Another back-breaking moment was when France got called for two flagrants in a single play at the end of the third quarter, which resulted in a five-point possession for the United States and extended its lead to 73-57 going into the fourth.

"We have to give France a lot of credit," Clark said. "They play with a lot of grit. They play with a lot of passion. They're aggressive. But I think we showed what wearing a USA jersey is all about. It's about dominating, and that's exactly what we did."

Did it hurt that France wasn't tested until the gold medal game?

Voepel: This wasn't a tight game down to the wire in which France might have needed that experience. However, where it perhaps cost the French is that they hadn't faced a defense as good as what Team USA threw at them in the third quarter. France had been especially good all tournament from behind the arc, and it again reached double-digit 3-pointers with 11 on Sunday. But the French went from 8-of-14 from 3-point range in the first half to 3-of-10 in the second.

And Gabby Williams, who had been a force all tournament, went from 16 points in the first half to four in the second. Marine Johannes, one of France's main sharpshooters, had just one 3-pointer in the game.

How well did Team USA's newcomers play?

Voepel: Overall, they did their jobs, and that says a lot when you add in the extra pressure of playing for your country. Tons of eyes were on Clark, of course, and she had a double-double in Team USA's opener vs. China. While she didn't shoot as well from 3-point range as she would have liked during the tournament (7-for-25, 28%), she was 2-of-3 from behind the arc Sunday and 4-of-5 from the field. She finished with 12 points and three assists and led Team USA in overall assists for the tournament with 32. Reese also made her presence felt, especially on the defensive end of the court where her size and quick hands flustered foes.

Guards Clark and Bueckers don't have anywhere near as much experience at the international level or in playing together as Gray and Young, who have been Las Vegas Aces teammates for six years with three WNBA titles. That helps explain why Lawson relied more on the vets during the most stressful periods in the Americans' close games but gave the youngsters playing time throughout the tournament so that the vets weren't worn out by the gold medal game.

Every Team USA basketball coach -- women's and men's -- is always heavily scrutinized for how they balance having so much talent and distributing minutes. In the end, give Lawson credit for how she allowed growth and important court time for the young players but also understood when veteran experience was what Team USA needed most.

Philippou: Taking the tournament as a whole, all of the young players had some really strong moments, showed where they have some room for growth and demonstrated the promise of what they might be able to do over time as a collective. And while Lawson relied heavily on the vets against France, what those younger players absorbed from the experience of playing for the senior national team and observing the older players is invaluable. With Team USA coming home with gold and its winning streak in major international tournaments intact, it was as good of a debut as could realistically be expected.

What does this win mean for Team USA?

Voepel: It's a new era for the world's dominant power in women's basketball but the same result. Team USA's last loss in a major international competition was in the 2006 World Cup semifinals to Russia. Before that, the most recent American losses were in the 1992 Olympic semifinals to what was then called the Unified Team (essentially the former Soviet Union with an interim name) and the 1994 World Cup semifinals to Brazil.

While we already noted Team USA's only major competition loss in a gold medal game came in the 1983 World Cup to the Soviet Union, the Americans have one other silver medal. That came in the 1976 Olympics, the first time the Summer Games had women's basketball. But that was a six-team round-robin tournament that the Soviets won by going 5-0. Team USA was 3-2 but took silver thanks to its round-robin win over fellow 3-2 team Bulgaria.

All that history is important to illustrate how outstanding Team USA has been in the Olympics and World Cup and to show what an upset it would have been had France taken the gold Sunday. It would have been just the third silver for Team USA.

All these World Cup players could be back in the mix for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, along with Wilson, Plum and up-and-coming younger standouts such as WNBA rookie Olivia Miles and college stars such as JuJu Watkins, Sarah Strong and Hannah Hidalgo. The pipeline for talent continues to be full.

Philippou: And yet the tournament reminded us that winning is hard, even as USA Basketball often makes it look easy, and it's getting even more difficult as the quality of play and teams improves globally.

Sue Bird, the managing director for the U.S. women's national team, made an interesting point in a pregame news conference: With more international players coming to the WNBA and getting plenty familiar with the Americans, the psychological factor of being intimidated by Team USA on a World Cup or Olympic stage won't be as prevalent. The United States won't be able to rest on its laurels if it wants to continue its run of dominance, and it'll be interesting to see how the U.S. women continue to evolve and grow.

What does the loss mean for France?

Voepel: The French wanted this very badly and played great for 5½ games in this tournament. But the second half Sunday was like the clock striking midnight on France's hopes. The French just couldn't match Team USA when the Americans went to their next gear. That said, look at the progress France has made internationally and in the WNBA; 13 French players have been on WNBA rosters this season. The sky is the limit for a youngster like Seattle Storm center Dominique Malonga (21 points, six rebounds Sunday). France lost by just one point to the United States in the 2024 Olympic final in Paris and now takes silver in the World Cup.

Add that to Spain's bronze medal and host Germany's fourth-place finish, and it's an excellent showing for Europe, whose players have become a significantly bigger factor in helping the WNBA improve its talent level and global footprint. Plus, France and the rest of Europe will be all the more motivated for the Los Angeles Games in two years.

stories.headline: Arsenal's Gabriel 'eager' to take another Champions League final penalty: 'If it happens again, I'll be there'
stories.summary: Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final.
stories.body:
Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said told ESPN that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final after the heartbreak of missing the crucial spot kick in last season's final against Paris Saint-Germain.

Following an earlier miss from Eberechi Eze in the shootout, Arsenal's hopes of winning their first European trophy rested on the shoulders of the Brazil defender who ultimately sent the ball over the crossbar to crown PSG champions for a second consecutive season.

Gabriel, a stalwart character of the Arsenal defence, told ESPN Brasil that if he was in a similar position again, he would take another penalty.

"I couldn't let a single missed penalty erase everything I'd achieved during the season," he said.

"So, I just thank God for the opportunity to have been there in that moment, it's part of the football.

"But I'm definitely eager for another chance, if it happens again, I'll be there, and if I have to take the penalty, I'll take it. So, that's it."

Arsenal were praised throughout last season's campaign for their solid defence, conceding just seven goals throughout their European campaign.

Gabriel thanked the fans for their continued support despite their European season ending on a sour note.

"I only have to thank the fans," he told ESPN Brasil. "Ever since the final, I've just received a lot of support from them, you know. They were incredible to me, sending very positive messages.

"But like I said, it's part of football. I'm here, and it's not the first time something like this has happened. So, as I said, if there's another penalty for me to take, I'll take it."

Despite the missed opportunity in the Champions League final, Arsenal did end their 22-year wait for the Premier League title and look as though their form is continuing on into this campaign.

Mikel Arteta's side are yet to drop points this season but face a stiff test when they take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light on Saturday.

stories.headline: Cleary avoids ban, but drama far from over
stories.summary: Penrith's hopes of a fifth premiership in six years could again hinge on Nathan Cleary's fitness, after his joy at avoiding a finals ban was dampened by confirmation of bone damage in his foot.
stories.body:
Penrith's hopes of a fifth premiership in six years could again hinge on Nathan Cleary's fitness, after his joy at avoiding a finals ban was dampened by confirmation of bone damage in his foot.

Cleary was on Monday handed a grade-one dangerous contact charge for collecting Hugo Savala's leg after the Sydney Rooster kicked in Penrith's 19-12 qualifying-final win.

That charge only carries with it a $1000 fine with an early guilty plea, meaning Cleary can breathe a sigh of relief with no ban.

But the bigger issue is now Cleary's foot, after Penrith confirmed he had "sustained a stress-related bone issue in his foot".

Cleary had appeared to tell a Panthers physio it was "f---ed" soon after kicking his match-winning field goal in Sunday's victory.

The two-time Clive Churchill Medallist had scans on Monday, with Penrith now tight-lipped on Cleary's exact path forward..

"Cleary will continue to be assessed and monitored by the Panthers medical team," the Panthers said in a statement.

It would likely take astronomical damage for Cleary to miss Penrith's preliminary final, or grand final if they again win through to the decider.

The Panthers have the best part of two weeks to rest up before taking on the Warriors or Newcastle, and the star halfback could take a pain-killing injection if required.

Penrith are also no strangers to having men play through injury in vital games.

Cleary's co-captain Isaah Yeo is playing this finals series after delaying surgery on a ruptured pec, while fullback Dylan Edwards soldiered on with a broken foot in 2021.

Cleary himself battled on after a dislocated shoulder in 2021, and needed shoulder surgery again when Penrith lifted their fourth straight title in 2024.

READ: NRL 2026 team-by-team season review

Penrith's title runs have often hinged on Cleary's foot. His kicking has been key in all four of premierships.

But the bigger question would likely be how much the injury or any treatment impacts Cleary's ability to run, step and kick through the rest of this finals series.

In the unlikely event Cleary is out, Penrith have Jack Cogger returning from suspension for the preliminary final, with Jack Cole having been solid at No.6.

Blaize Talagi could also return to the halves. He filled in at centre on Sunday after being dropped last month.

"It's incredible the depth we have," second-rower Liam Martin said.

"Jack's (Cole) been unbelievable the last three weeks. His defence has been incredibly strong, his attack, his running game.

"He's playing with such confidence. It's awesome to see. He's always had the talent and worked hard. I'm really glad to see him get his chance."

Meanwhile, the match review committee's call to hand Cleary a grade-one charge saved Penrith weighing up a monumental decision.

Had Cleary been handed a grade-two charge, the Penrith halfback would have been facing a one-game ban and the reality of being rubbed out of the preliminary final.

If Penrith had fought the charge and lost, that ban would have extended to the grand final.

Manly prop Josh Aloiai and South Sydney forward Jacob Host received grade-two charges in 2024 for making contact with kickers.

Canberra's Zac Hosking was fined for a similar incident in last year's finals, while Melbourne's Harry Grant had a charge overturned at the judiciary in 2024.

Speaking before Cleary escaped with a fine, Cronulla half Nicho Hynes called for consistency.

"Sometimes people get suspended for it, sometimes you won't," Hynes said.

"I love Nathan and he's a really good guy and you don't want to see your best players getting stamped out of the final series.

"But whatever's warranted is warranted. As long as it's equal for every player across the board, then that's all that matters.

"You've got to treat everyone the same, regardless of whether you're the face of the game or you're not."
